steps.text: What this is. Every move from 4,605 of your Lichess 3+2 games (2,225 of them losses), sorted by things you can see during a game: material, clocks, whether queens are on. Then every mistake placed on a scale from “obvious next move” to “only an engine would know.”

What counts as a mistake. Your expected result is how often you score from a position, given the engine's evaluation and both clocks. The model behind it was fitted on your own games, so it knows your real conversion rate. A move is a mistake if it drops your expected result by 10 points or more, for example from 60% to 50%.

Clocks matter here. With both players short of time, the same engine drop counts about 15–20% less, because a low clock makes any position less certain.

Material is what you would count at the board: pawn 1, knight or bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. A trade that's half done counts as level: if they just took a piece you can take straight back, that piece is counted as back.

Engine numbers are in pawns from your side: +1.0 means about a pawn better for you. Every engine number on these cards is a fresh Stockfish check at depth 18, deeper than the depth-12 numbers used to find the examples.

The examples are three lost games per point, picked at random from the ones that fit and kept only if the deeper check agreed. Each has a Lichess link that opens just before the move.

Being a pawn or two up is where you make mistakes most often.

In your lost games, up 1–2 pawns is 12.5% of your moves but 25% of the damage. You make a mistake about once every 5 moves there (21 per 100), against once every 8 when material is even (13 per 100). The average one costs 23 points of expected result.

It's the state that feels safest, and it's the most mistake-dense one you have. These mistakes come in every kind: about a quarter lose material within three moves, and the rest don't show up as material straight away.

Game 1 of 3. Move 32, you're Black. Lost: you were checkmated on move 66. Open it on Lichess (opens just before the move).

At the board: you have two knights against their a rook, so up 1 on the count. Clocks: you 0:23, them 0:35. Queens off.

They had just played R3e2. You played Nf4 (black arrow). The engine's move was h5 (blue arrow).

Engine: +2.2 before your move, -4.3 after it. Your expected result: 55%, then 17%.

The punishment the engine sees (red arrow): 33. Rxe7+ Kg6 34. Rd1 Ne6

In the game: 33. Rxe7+ Kg6 34. Kg1. By your next turn you were down 2, so this one announced itself.

Game 2 of 3. Move 10, you're Black. Lost: you resigned on move 41. Open it on Lichess (opens just before the move).

At the board: you have a knight against their two pawns, so up 1 on the count. Clocks: you 2:17, them 2:28. Queens on.

They had just played Bd3. You played Nf6 (black arrow). The engine's move was Bxe4 (blue arrow).

Engine: +1.9 before your move, -5.2 after it. Your expected result: 60%, then 14%.

The punishment the engine sees (red arrow): 11. Nxf6+ gxf6 12. Bxf5 Nd7

In the game: 11. Nxf6+ gxf6 12. Bxf5. By your next turn material was still up 1: nothing told you anything had happened.

Game 3 of 3. Move 23, you're White. Lost: you resigned on move 48. Open it on Lichess (opens just before the move).

At the board: you're up a pawn. Clocks: you 0:43, them 0:05. Queens off.

They had just played Rhe8. You played Ne6+ (black arrow). The engine's move was Rfc1 (blue arrow).

Engine: +1.9 before your move, -4.9 after it. Your expected result: 77%, then 41%.

The punishment the engine sees (red arrow): 23...Bxe6 24. Bxe6 Rxe6 25. Rad1

In the game: 23...Bxe6 24. Bxe6 Rxe6. By your next turn you were down 2, so this one announced itself.

So what. “I'm a pawn up” is a signal you can actually read during a game, and it's the moment your error rate is highest. That's the conversion problem from earlier work, now in terms you can see at the board.

cards.t: Ahead by a pawn or two

steps.text:
When you're up a piece or more, your mistakes are rarer but the largest of all.

In lost games, up a piece or more is 5% of your moves and 11% of the damage. The average mistake there costs 30 points, more than anywhere else.

The typical one is handing material straight back. 37% of your mistakes made a piece up lose material within three moves, the highest share of any material state. In all three games below the opponent took it on the very next move.

At the board: material is even until you take back the piece they just captured; after that you're up 3. Clocks: you 2:02, them 2:00. Queens on.

Engine: +2.9 before your move, -0.0 after it. Your expected result: 68%, then 46%.
They replied fxg3 (red arrow) and took it. At your next turn you were even on the count, against up 3 before your move. No doubt about this one: it showed up the very next move.

cards.t: Up a piece: the biggest mistakes

steps.text:
Even material carries its fair share of the damage, and the single worst move most often.

Even material is 34% of moves in your lost games and 36% of the damage, about par. But take the one costliest move of each lost game: 41% of them were played at even material, and 33% at even material with queens on.

In 72% of those, the engine called the position roughly level beforehand (your chances between 35% and 65%). The game was there to be played, and one move gave it away. The three games below are exactly that: the costliest move of each.

cards.t: Even material: where the worst move happens

With queens on, you make mistakes almost twice as often.

In lost games, positions with both queens on are 57% of your moves but 72% of the damage: 14 mistakes per 100 moves against 8 with queens off. Three in four of the costliest moves of your lost games came with queens on.

For the examples I picked games where the engine's punishment starts with their queen. That's the thing to see in each: what their queen can reach after your move.

Being ahead or behind on the clock barely changes how often you make mistakes.

Mistakes per 100 moves in lost games: 9.1 with you under 20 seconds, 10.9 when you're 30+ seconds behind, 11.6 when clocks are within 30 seconds, 13.7 when you're 30+ seconds ahead. If anything, more when ahead on time.

Under 20 seconds you make fewer mistakes per move but bigger ones: 24.5 points on average, against about 21 otherwise. Part of “fewer” is the measure itself: it discounts mistakes when clocks are low.

The examples are big mistakes under 20 seconds, from positions the engine liked for you. They're real, but they're not where most of your losses come from.

cards.t: The clock gap mostly doesn't matter

steps.text:
Your mistakes when a piece or more down barely register, and that isn't good defence.

In lost games, down a piece or more is 26.5% of your moves but only 5.7% of the damage (2.6 mistakes per 100 moves).

By then your expected result is already close to zero, so a further mistake has little left to take away. That's why there are no examples here: this point is about the measure, not about a kind of mistake.

cards.t: Down a piece: little left to lose

steps.text:
These are the mistakes you'd know about straight away, and they do the most damage.

To place each mistake on the scale, I had the engine play the game on 15 moves from your move and from its own best move, and compared the material.

In 24% of your mistakes you lose material or get mated within three moves. They are 41% of the damage in your lost games and the biggest per mistake (29 points). When the material could be taken on the very next move, real opponents took it 71% of the time.

These are the hangs the two looks are aimed at. In the three games below, the opponent took it on the next move.

cards.t: Seen at once: material gone within 3 moves

steps.text:
12% of your mistakes are chances you didn't take, and these never feel like mistakes.

The opponent left something you could have won within three moves, and you played something else. You lost nothing you could count, so nothing bad happens on the board. They are 11% of the damage in your lost games.

Catching these means asking the mirror image of Look 1: not “what can they take?” but “what did their move leave that I can take?”

Game 1 of 3. Move 17, you're Black. Lost: you lost on time on move 45. Open it on Lichess (opens just before the move).

At the board: you have a knight against their a bishop, so even on the count. Clocks: you 2:53, them 2:54. Queens on.

They had just played Rb1. You played Rb8 (black arrow). The engine's move was Nxb2 (blue arrow).

Engine: +5.5 before your move, +1.6 after it. Your expected result: 82%, then 58%.

What was there. The win took 2 moves to collect. The line: 17...Nxb2 18. Rxb2 Rxc3 19. Be2. After it you'd have been up 3 on the count, against even before.

What you played lost nothing you could count: on the engine's line after your move, material stays within a pawn of where it was. So nothing on the board told you a chance had gone.

Engine: -0.4 before your move, -6.1 after it. Your expected result: 21%, then 4%.

What was there. The engine's move was a capture you could make right away. The line: 30...Bxa1 31. Bc5. After it you'd have been up 1 on the count, against down 4 before.

What you played lost nothing you could count: on the engine's line after your move, material stays within a pawn of where it was. So nothing on the board told you a chance had gone.

They had just played Rxf4. You played Bxf4 (black arrow). The engine's move was e5 (blue arrow).

Engine: +3.4 before your move, -1.8 after it. Your expected result: 72%, then 36%.

What was there. The win took 3 moves to collect. The line: 22...e5 23. Qc3 Bxf4 24. dxe5 Re8 25. e6. After it you'd have been up 3 on the count, against even before.

What you played lost nothing you could count: on the engine's line after your move, material stays within a pawn of where it was. So nothing on the board told you a chance had gone.

A third of your mistakes only cost material much later, and most of that third is really positional.

In 33% of your mistakes, the engine's line wins material from you only 4 to 15 moves on. A caution before reading too much into that: when I ran the same test on good moves, 20% landed here too. Engine lines that long drift.

So read this group as mostly positional, with some real delayed tactics mixed in. The three below are the real kind: in each, the loss holds up when the engine plays the line out.

They are 22% of the damage in your lost games. With the 4–15-move group, which is mostly the same thing, this is the part of your mistakes that no check for hanging pieces will ever reach.

Altogether, about two-thirds of your mistakes, and a bit over half of the damage, give no material signal for at least three moves.

Your hunch was right: when the opponent's mistake leaves nothing to grab, you often don't notice it happened.

After an opponent's mistake that leaves material you can win, you give much of the advantage back 18% of the time. After one that leaves nothing you can take, 35% of the time. On an ordinary move at the same evaluation, the rate is 6–15%.

I re-checked 500 of these with a deeper engine to rule out a measurement artifact, and the gap held. Some of it is that these positions often need one exact move. But the size of the gap fits “didn't register that anything changed.”

cards.t: After their mistake, when nothing can be taken

steps.text:
After a mistake of yours, the next move is about twice as likely to be one too, whether or not you could have seen the first.

Your next move is 1.5–2 times as likely to be a mistake as normal for its position. It's 2.0 times after mistakes that lost material within three moves, and 1.8 times after mistakes that never cost material at all.

So it isn't a reaction to noticing a blunder; you can't react to what you didn't see. More likely the position is harder, or the same blind spot is still there.

Game 1 of 3. Move 30, you're White. Lost: you resigned on move 35. Open it on Lichess (opens just before the move).

At the board: you have a rook against their a bishop and two pawns, so even on the count. Clocks: you 1:43, them 1:47. Queens on.

They had just played Qh3+. You played Ke2 (black arrow). The engine's move was Kf2 (blue arrow).

Engine: -0.1 before your move, -6.0 after it. Your expected result: 45%, then 12%.

One move later. They played Bh5. You played Kd2 (black arrow); the engine's move was Kf2 (blue arrow).

Engine: -0.6 before, -5.3 after. Your expected result: 41%, then 15%. Two mistakes in a row.

Game 2 of 3. Move 20, you're Black. Lost: you resigned on move 41. Open it on Lichess (opens just before the move).

At the board: you have a bishop against their a knight and a pawn, so down 1 on the count. Clocks: you 2:02, them 2:24. Queens on.

They had just played Qf2. You played bxc6 (black arrow). The engine's move was Re2 (blue arrow).

Engine: -0.2 before your move, -5.4 after it. Your expected result: 43%, then 13%.

One move later. They played Rf1. You played c5 (black arrow); the engine's move was g6 (blue arrow).

Engine: -2.5 before, -5.7 after. Your expected result: 26%, then 12%. Two mistakes in a row.

Game 3 of 3. Move 16, you're White. Lost: you resigned on move 41. Open it on Lichess (opens just before the move).

At the board: material is even. Clocks: you 2:07, them 2:05. Queens on.

They had just played h5. You played d6 (black arrow). The engine's move was h4 (blue arrow).

Engine: +3.0 before your move, +0.0 after it. Your expected result: 68%, then 46%.

One move later. They played exd6. You played Ne4 (black arrow); the engine's move was Bh4 (blue arrow).

Engine: +1.2 before, -2.3 after. Your expected result: 52%, then 27%. Two mistakes in a row.

Exploratory, not a test set up in advance. The cut points (a pawn or two, 20 seconds, three moves) were chosen once and not tuned, but nothing here was pre-registered.

About 1 in 5 mistakes shrinks below the 10-point line when re-checked with a deeper engine (82% hold up). The 15-move engine lines get fuzzy toward the end, which is why the 4–15-move group gets a caution.

Three examples per point show what each kind looks like. They don't prove the numbers; the numbers come from thousands of moves.
